chapter.title: Typing Props
chapter.description: The base patterns for component props, including children.

blocks.text: A component's props are just an object, so you type them like any other object. Most codebases declare an interface or a type alias and annotate the parameter.

For props either works. `interface` can be extended and merged; `type` can express unions and intersections. Pick one for consistency - many teams use `interface` for props and `type` for everything else.
`ReactNode` covers everything React can render: elements, strings, numbers, arrays, `null` and `undefined`.

`React.FC` used to be the standard way to type a component and implicitly added `children`. It no longer does in React 18 types, and it makes generic components awkward. Annotate the props parameter directly instead.
A wrapper component should usually accept everything the underlying element does. `ComponentProps` pulls those types in for you.

next.title: Typing Hooks
next.description: Where inference is enough and where you need to help it.

blocks.text: TypeScript infers the type from the initial value, which covers most cases. Supply a type argument when the initial value does not describe the full range.
`useState([])` infers `never[]`, so pushing anything into it is an error. Always supply the element type for an empty array.
The two uses of `useRef` need different types, and the difference matters.
Type the state and the action union, and the reducer's exhaustiveness comes free.
With a discriminated union, TypeScript narrows `action` inside each case, so `action.value` is only available where it exists. Miss a case and the return type check catches it.

blocks.caption: The runtime guard also removes null from the type for every caller.
